proposed.text: Architect C prepared design plans for a shopping mall but the project was cancelled before construction began. Five years later, a real estate company obtained copies of these plans and used them to construct an identical shopping mall in a different province. What is Architect C's strongest legal position?

options.text: Architect C cannot claim ownership because the original project was never built
Architect C must prove actual intent to harm before Section 33 can apply
Architect C retains ownership unless a written stipulation provides otherwise, and unauthorized use for another project violates the written-consent rule
Architect C's rights expired after three years without construction

rationale.a: Incorrectly conditions copyright on project execution; the statute explicitly protects the architect's intellectual property whether the building is built or not.
rationale.b: Misunderstands copyright infringement standards; the infringer's intent is irrelevant; unauthorized reproduction alone constitutes infringement.
rationale.d: Falsely imposes a time limit on copyright; RA 9266 Section 33 contains no expiration based on time without project execution.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 33 explicitly protects the architect's intellectual property 'whether the object for which they are made is executed or not.' The copyright ownership is not conditional on project execution or time. The architect retains full rights to pursue infringement remedies regardless of whether the original commission was ever built or how many years have passed.
rationale.takeaway: An architect's copyright protection continues indefinitely even if the original commissioned project is never executed or is abandoned.

proposed.explanation: Source-audited against RA 9266 IRR Sections 3(27), 3(32), 20(4), and 33; the answer turns on retained copyright ownership, original-project use, and written consent for repetition or other projects.
